questions.question: What is the & (symbol-to-proc) shorthand in Ruby?
questions.title: Symbol to Proc (&)
questions.direct_answer: The &:sym shorthand converts a symbol to a block that calls that method on each element: names.map(&:upcase) is names.map { |n| n.upcase }. The & before a symbol (or any object with to_proc) turns it into a block, and the symbol's to_proc returns a proc that sends the method to its argument. It's a concise idiom for 'call this method on each item' — common with map, select, sort_by — and reads cleanly once you know it. It's not magic: &:upcase is just shorthand for the block { |x| x.upcase }.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know &:upcase is shorthand for { |x| x.upcase } and that & turns an object with to_proc into a block.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using &:method when you need arguments or a transformation beyond a single method call (it won't fit).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: &:upcase is shorthand for { |x| x.upcase }; & turns a symbol (via to_proc) into a block. Used with map/select/sort_by for 'call this method on each item'.

sections.title: Concise 'Call This Method On Each Item'
sections.content: The ampersand-colon shorthand converts a symbol to a block that calls that method on each element: names.map(&:upcase) is the same as names.map { |n| n.upcase }. The ampersand before a symbol, or any object with a to_proc method, turns it into a block, and the symbol's to_proc returns a proc that sends the method to its argument. It's a concise idiom for 'call this method on each item' — common with map, select, sort_by, and flat_map — and reads cleanly once you know it. It's not magic: ampersand-colon-upcase is just shorthand for the block that calls upcase on each element.

sections.title: Symbol -> Proc -> Block
sections.content:
&:upcase becomes { |x| x.upcase } via to_proc.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Symbol :upcase] -->|& + to_proc| P[proc { |x| x.upcase }]
  P -->|as block| M[map calls it on each element]
```

sections.title: Symbol to proc
sections.content:
```ruby
# These two are equivalent:
names = %w[ada bob cara]
names.map(&:upcase)            # ['ADA', 'BOB', 'CARA']
names.map { |n| n.upcase }     # same thing, spelled out

# Common uses:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.map(&:to_s)               # ['1', '2', '3']
nums.select(&:even?)           # [2]
nums.sort_by(&:abs)            # sort by absolute value
users.map(&:name)              # call .name on each user

# It works because Symbol#to_proc returns a proc that sends the method:
#   :upcase.to_proc  # -> proc { |obj| obj.upcase }

# Limit: only for a single method with no args:
nums.map(&:to_s)               # ok
# nums.map(&:to_s(2))          # NO - can't pass args this way
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using &:method when you need arguments (it only calls a single no-arg method).
Not recognizing it as shorthand (it looks cryptic until you know to_proc).
Confusing & (to-proc, before a symbol/obj) with & in a method signature (splat of block arg).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: &:upcase is shorthand for { |x| x.upcase } — call that method on each element.
& before a symbol turns it into a block via the symbol's to_proc.
Common with map, select, sort_by for 'call this method on each item'.
Only works for a single method with no arguments (no &:to_s(2)).
It's not magic — it's the block { |x| x.upcase } written concisely.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: The ampersand-colon shorthand converts a symbol to a block that calls that method on each element: names dot map ampersand colon upcase is the same as names dot map with n n dot upcase. The ampersand before a symbol, or any object with a to_proc method, turns it into a block, and the symbol's to_proc returns a proc that sends the method to its argument. It's a concise idiom for call this method on each item — common with map, select, sort_by, and flat_map — and reads cleanly once you know it. It's not magic: ampersand-colon-upcase is just shorthand for the block that calls upcase on each element. A limitation is that it only works for a single method with no arguments, so you can't pass args this way. A common mistake is not recognizing it as shorthand, because it looks cryptic until you know to_proc.
